title: Parasites in the Toolchain: A Large-Scale Analysis of Attacks on the MCP Ecosystem
pdf_path: papers/Parasites in the Toolchain_A Large-Scale Analysis of Attacks on the MCP Ecosystem.pdf
threat_model_summary: Attacker does not deploy a malicious server or contact the victim directly; it plants instructions in external content that a benign agent retrieves during normal tasks, then composes legitimate MCP tools through external ingestion, private-data read and network exfiltration.
core_contributions: Parasitic Toolchain Attack / MCP-UPD
Measurement of 1,360 servers and 12,230 tools; 8.7% of tools and 27.2% of servers dynamically exploitable
End-to-end tool-chain validation: 9 of 10 chains succeeded at least once
Shows model/client dependence and proposes context-tool isolation and least-privilege defenses
limitations: Defenses proposed but not implemented or evaluated
Success varies strongly by LLM and client
Measurement limited to sampled ecosystems and prompts
No formal security model
No cryptographic mechanism
theoretical_crypto_links: None; capability means tool functionality, not cryptographic capability
Task-bound, attenuable authorization credentials are our inference only
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, authentication protocol, TEE or ZK
Server identity/signing and log integrity do not stop semantic instruction/data confusion (our inference)
evidence_refs: pp.1-5 attack model and three stages

title: “Do Not Mention This to the User”: Detecting and Understanding Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild
pdf_path: papers/“Do Not Mention This to the User”_Detecting and Understanding Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild.pdf
threat_model_summary: Malicious skill publishers distribute skills through public marketplaces; users install them into coding agents. Skills can read credentials, execute code, manipulate the agent and hide behavior; the study measures real-world prevalence and behavior rather than modeling a cryptographic adversary.
core_contributions: First large-scale behaviorally confirmed dataset of malicious Agent Skills
98,380 skills crawled; 157 malicious skills and 632 vulnerabilities confirmed
84.2% of vulnerabilities are in natural-language SKILL.md documentation
Two negatively correlated families: Data Thieves and Agent Hijackers; one publisher accounts for 54.1%
limitations: Snapshot of two marketplaces in January 2026
Dynamic verification limited to 60-second Docker windows
Some reported precision/FP numbers do not fully reconcile (our audit)
Detection is pattern/LLM-based and can be evaded
No formal security model
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic construction, definition or proof
Skill provenance signatures/transparency logs and remote attestation are our inference
applied_crypto_links: Credentials and API keys are stolen assets, not mechanisms
No signing, scoped tokens, attestation or key management implemented

title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
pdf_path: papers/Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses.pdf
threat_model_summary: Attacker can modify only the external data processed by the application, not the application's instruction prompt; backend LLM is intact. Single-turn, no tool calls, no memory. The formalization is a functional notation for attack construction, not a cryptographic security game.
core_contributions: Functional formalization unifying naive, escape-character, context-ignoring and fake-completion attacks
Combined Attack derived from the formalization
Benchmark of 10 LLMs x 7 NLP tasks x 49 target/injected combinations
Systematic evaluation of five defenses showing all are insufficient
limitations: No security definition, advantage, theorem or reduction
Attacker model does not include target instruction in the attack function
Single-turn and no tool/memory setting
Small evaluation samples and no confidence intervals
Defenses evaluated only empirically
theoretical_crypto_links: None; 'formalizing' means mathematical notation for attack construction
Authenticated instruction provenance is our inference, and cannot ensure semantic obedience
applied_crypto_links: No signatures, MACs, TEE, credentials or encryption
Provenance/authentication of data sources is at most a peripheral interface (our inference)
evidence_refs: pp.8-10 attack results and model-size correlation

title: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
pdf_path: papers/StruQ_Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries.pdf
threat_model_summary: Application developer controls the prompt channel; user data is untrusted and may contain injected instructions. A trusted front-end encodes channels with reserved tokens and filters forged delimiters; the model is trained to obey only the prompt channel. No cryptographic adversary model.
core_contributions: Structured queries separating prompt and data channels with reserved tokens
Recursive filtering of delimiter-forging strings
Structured instruction tuning from a base LLM
Evaluation against handcrafted and optimization-based injections on Llama-7B and Mistral-7B
limitations: Only programmatic API settings, not chatbots, tool calls, multi-turn or agents
GCG still achieves 58% ASR on Llama
Filtering silently removes data substrings and may harm data integrity
No formal guarantee
Requires model fine-tuning
theoretical_crypto_links: None; channel separation is parsing/training, not cryptographic authentication
Data provenance and capability tokens are our inference and only peripheral
applied_crypto_links: No keys, signatures, MACs, commitments, ZK, MPC or TEE
Reserved-token separation is not cryptographic domain separation

title: Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: No-box attacker publishes one malicious tool document in an open tool marketplace; it does not know the target task description, retriever, target LLM, tool library or top-k. Goal: make the agent consistently select the malicious tool for an attacker-chosen target task.
core_contributions: ToolHijacker, a no-box prompt injection attack on two-stage tool selection
Formalizes malicious tool-document crafting as an optimization problem
Decomposes into retrieval and selection objectives with R+S subsequence optimization
Gradient-free and gradient-based solvers; up to 99.6% ASR across 8 LLMs and 4 retrievers
limitations: Evaluated on MetaTool/ToolBench-style retrieval, not all agent frameworks
Defenses evaluated are insufficient but not exhaustive
No formal security model
Attack assumes marketplace acceptance of malicious tool documents
No cryptographic mechanism
theoretical_crypto_links: None; optimization-based adversarial ML, not cryptographic
Tool provenance and signed manifests are our inference and cannot ensure selection semantics
applied_crypto_links: No signatures, credentials, TEE or encryption
Marketplace moderation and retrieval integrity are system-level, not cryptographic
